title: Mode collapse in traditional GANs
description: The paper states that the mode dropping phenomenon (mode collapse) is typical in GANs, and is drastically reduced by WGAN.
canonical_description: mode collapse is a common failure mode in traditional generative adversarial networks

evidence.anchor: mode dropping phenomenon that is typical in GANs
evidence.quote:
The mode dropping
  phenomenon that is typical in GANs is also drastically reduced.

verdict.reasoning: Four papers directly and explicitly address the mode collapse problem in traditional GANs, each proposing a principled solution with theoretical grounding and empirical validation. Paper 1 (Primal-Dual Subgradient) shows both standard GAN and WGAN fail on a toy example while their method succeeds, and demonstrates full mode coverage on synthetic mixtures and MNIST. Paper 3 (Distribution Fitting) provides theoretical proof that the GAN objective can be minimized even when distributions differ (causing collapse), and proposes GDF/LDF penalties that preserve the global minimum while preventing collapse; validated across multiple datasets. Paper 4 (MR-GAN) adds manifold regularization and shows the original GAN collapses to 7/8 Gaussian modes while MR-GAN captures all 8, with theoretical proofs of stability. Paper 5 (IVGAN) introduces an intervention loss equivalent to multi-distribution JS-divergence that provides richer gradients, capturing all 1,000 modes on stacked MNIST — a direct benchmark for mode coverage. Paper 2 (DRAGAN) is the only non-addressed assessment, as it focuses on stability rather than mode collapse. Collectively, these direct solutions cover the gap from multiple angles (optimization, distribution matching, manifold geometry, gradient informativeness), leaving little of the core problem unaddressed beyond inevitable refinements (e.g., scalability to extremely high dimensions).

paper.title: Training Generative Adversarial Networks via Primal-Dual Subgradient Methods: A Lagrangian Perspective on GAN
paper.abstract: We relate the minimax game of generative adversarial networks (GANs) to finding the saddle points of the Lagrangian function for a convex optimization problem, where the discriminator outputs and the distribution of generator outputs play the roles of primal variables and dual variables, respectively. This formulation shows the connection between the standard GAN training process and the primal-dual subgradient methods for convex optimization. The inherent connection does not only provide a theoretical convergence proof for training GANs in the function space, but also inspires a novel objective function for training. The modified objective function forces the distribution of generator outputs to be updated along the direction according to the primal-dual subgradient methods. A toy example shows that the proposed method is able to resolve mode collapse, which in this case cannot be avoided by the standard GAN or Wasserstein GAN. Experiments on both Gaussian mixture synthetic data and real-world image datasets demonstrate the performance of the proposed method on generating diverse samples.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper directly addresses mode collapse in GANs by reformulating GAN training as a primal-dual subgradient method for convex optimization. It identifies that standard GAN training fails to update the generated distribution at data support points when the supports are disjoint — a key cause of mode collapse. The paper proposes a modified generator loss function that adds a regularization term pushing the generated distribution toward the optimal update direction derived from primal-dual theory. A toy example (data at x=1, generator stuck at x=0) proves that standard GAN and WGAN both fail while the proposed method succeeds. Experiments on synthetic data (mixture of 8 Gaussians, 1000-class MNIST) show the method generates diverse samples across all modes, and quantitative results on MNIST and CIFAR-10 show improved inception scores.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fully addresses the gap of mode collapse in traditional GANs from a theoretical and algorithmic standpoint. It provides a principled solution with convergence guarantees in function space, demonstrates on a toy example where both GAN and WGAN fail, and shows empirical diversity improvements. The main limitation acknowledged is that the kernel density estimation for the generated distribution may suffer from the curse of dimensionality for high-dimensional data, though the paper suggests using autoencoder projections as a workaround. The paper does not claim state-of-the-art image quality but rather focuses on resolving mode collapse specifically.
evidence_snippets: A toy example reveals that for some cases when standard GAN or WGAN inevitably leads to mode collapse, our proposed method can effectively avoid mode collapse and converge to the optimal point.

Mode collapse occurs when the generated samples have a very small probability to overlap with some families of the data samples, and the discriminator D(·) is locally constant around the region of the generated samples. We use a toy example to show that the standard training of GAN and Wasserstein may fail to avoid mode collapse, while our proposed method can succeed.
While the original GANs experience mode collapse, our proposed method is able to generate samples over all 8 modes.

paper.title: On Convergence and Stability of GANs
paper.abstract: We propose studying GAN training dynamics as regret minimization, which is in contrast to the popular view that there is consistent minimization of a divergence between real and generated distributions. We analyze the convergence of GAN training from this new point of view to understand why mode collapse happens. We hypothesize the existence of undesirable local equilibria in this non-convex game to be responsible for mode collapse. We observe that these local equilibria often exhibit sharp gradients of the discriminator function around some real data points. We demonstrate that these degenerate local equilibria can be avoided with a gradient penalty scheme called DRAGAN. We show that DRAGAN enables faster training, achieves improved stability with fewer mode collapses, and leads to generator networks with better modeling performance across a variety of architectures and objective functions.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper "On Convergence and Stability of GANs" studies the convergence and stability properties of GAN training, proposing a new regularization method (DRAGAN) to avoid local Nash equilibria and improve training stability. It does not specifically address the mode collapse problem or propose solutions for it.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not address mode collapse in traditional GANs at all. It focuses on training stability and convergence to local Nash equilibria, not on the mode dropping phenomenon. The gap of mode collapse reduction (e.g., via WGAN) remains entirely open and unaddressed by this paper.

paper.title: Distribution Fitting for Combating Mode Collapse in Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: Mode collapse is a significant unsolved issue of generative adversarial networks. In this work, we examine the causes of mode collapse from a novel perspective. Due to the nonuniform sampling in the training process, some sub-distributions may be missed when sampling data. As a result, even when the generated distribution differs from the real one, the GAN objective can still achieve the minimum. To address the issue, we propose a global distribution fitting (GDF) method with a penalty term to confine the generated data distribution. When the generated distribution differs from the real one, GDF will make the objective harder to reach the minimal value, while the original global minimum is not changed. To deal with the circumstance when the overall real data is unreachable, we also propose a local distribution fitting (LDF) method. Experiments on several benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and competitive performance of GDF and LDF.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper directly addresses mode collapse in traditional GANs by proposing Global Distribution Fitting (GDF) and Local Distribution Fitting (LDF) methods. The key insight is that nonuniform sampling during training causes the GAN objective to reach its minimum even when the generated distribution differs from the real one, leading to mode collapse. GDF adds a penalty term that constrains the mean and standard deviation of generated data to match those of the real data, while LDF uses running estimates when the full real distribution is unavailable. The paper provides theoretical proofs that the global minimum remains unchanged while making it harder to reach the minimum when distributions differ, and demonstrates effectiveness on synthetic data, Stacked MNIST, CIFAR-10, STL-10, and Tiny-ImageNet.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fully addresses the gap of mode collapse in traditional GANs by proposing and validating a specific solution. However, it acknowledges limitations: (1) the method requires large batch sizes, limiting applicability in settings like unpaired image-to-image translation or high-resolution synthesis on single GPUs; (2) mean and standard deviation only capture partial distribution information, which may be insufficient for high-dimensional data; (3) the theoretical analysis assumes linearly combined sub-distributions, and effectiveness for non-linearly combined mixed distributions is not thoroughly tested. These are refinements of the solution rather than an unaddressed gap.
evidence_snippets: Mode collapse is a significant unsolved issue of generative adversarial networks. In this work, we examine the causes of mode collapse from a novel perspective.

We propose global and local distribution fitting methods to suppress mode collapse. On the basis of not changing the global minimum of the GAN objective, the method will make the objective harder to reach the minimum when the generated distribution is not the same as the real one.
In Fig.~[REF:fig1], we observe that the original model suffers from severe mode collapse. Using GDF or LDF will inhibit mode collapse, and the network can learn a complete distribution.

paper.title: MR-GAN: Manifold Regularized Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: Despite the growing interest in generative adversarial networks (GANs), training GANs remains a challenging problem, both from a theoretical and a practical standpoint. To address this challenge, in this paper, we propose a novel way to exploit the unique geometry of the real data, especially the manifold information. More specifically, we design a method to regularize GAN training by adding an additional regularization term referred to as manifold regularizer. The manifold regularizer forces the generator to respect the unique geometry of the real data manifold and generate high quality data. Furthermore, we theoretically prove that the addition of this regularization term in any class of GANs including DCGAN and Wasserstein GAN leads to improved performance in terms of generalization, existence of equilibrium, and stability. Preliminary experiments show that the proposed manifold regularization helps in avoiding mode collapse and leads to stable training.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper proposes MR-GAN, which adds a manifold regularization term to the generator's objective function to force the generated data to respect the geometry of the real data manifold. The paper provides theoretical proofs that this regularization improves generalization, guarantees existence of equilibrium, and ensures exponentially stable training. Empirically, the paper demonstrates on a 2D mixture of 8 Gaussians that the original GAN collapses to 7 modes while MR-GAN captures all 8 modes, and shows quantitative improvements (Geometry Score) on MNIST and CelebA datasets over both DCGAN and WGAN baselines.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper directly addresses mode collapse in traditional GANs through its proposed manifold regularization method. The empirical results on the synthetic 2D Gaussian mixture clearly show that MR-GAN avoids the mode collapse that afflicts the original GAN. The paper also provides theoretical guarantees for stability and equilibrium existence. However, the paper does not claim to completely eliminate mode collapse in all settings — the experiments show improvement but not perfection (e.g., the Geometry Score on MNIST is improved but not zero). Additionally, the paper focuses on local (not global) convergence properties and leaves global convergence as future work.
evidence_snippets: Preliminary experiments show that the proposed manifold regularization helps in avoiding mode collapse and leads to stable training.

We can clearly observe from the comparison in the figure that the original GAN misses one of the 8 modes and the problem of mode collapse happens, and the proposed MR-GAN learns to evenly spread the probability mass and converges to all the 8 modes without any mode collapse.
Specifically, GAN training suffers from the following major problems: a) mode-collapse: the generator collapses with results in a poor generalization, i.e., producing limited varieties of samples

paper.title: Intervention Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: In this paper we propose a novel approach for stabilizing the training process of Generative Adversarial Networks as well as alleviating the mode collapse problem. The main idea is to introduce a regularization term that we call intervention loss into the objective. We refer to the resulting generative model as Intervention Generative Adversarial Networks (IVGAN). By perturbing the latent representations of real images obtained from an auxiliary encoder network with Gaussian invariant interventions and penalizing the dissimilarity of the distributions of the resulting generated images, the intervention loss provides more informative gradient for the generator, significantly improving GAN's training stability. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our methods via solid theoretical analysis and thorough evaluation on standard real-world datasets as well as the stacked MNIST dataset.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes Intervention GAN (IVGAN), which introduces an intervention loss (based on perturbing latent representations of real images with Gaussian-invariant interventions) and a reconstruction loss as regularizers to the standard GAN objective. The intervention loss is theoretically shown to be equivalent to a multi-distribution JS-divergence among intervened distributions that interpolate between the generated and data distributions, providing more informative gradients to the generator. The method is evaluated on standard datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, LSUN, STL-10) and the stacked MNIST dataset, where it captures all 1,000 modes, demonstrating effective alleviation of mode collapse.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fully addresses the gap of mode collapse in traditional GANs by proposing and empirically validating a method (IVGAN) that alleviates mode collapse. On the stacked MNIST benchmark, IVGAN captures all 1,000 modes, matching or exceeding state-of-the-art methods. The paper provides both theoretical analysis (showing the intervention loss provides more informative gradients than standard JS-divergence) and thorough empirical evaluation. No significant part of the gap remains unaddressed by this paper.
